prompt: In terraform plan output, what does a line prefixed with a plain + mean?
choices: It marks an attribute or resource that already exists and is unchanged.
It marks a resource or attribute that will be created.
It marks a resource that will be destroyed.
It marks a resource that will only be read, never modified.

prompt: What does a plan entry marked -/+ next to a resource mean?
choices: The resource will be destroyed and then recreated (replaced) because a change forces replacement.
The resource will be updated in place with no downtime.
The resource is being imported into state for the first time.
The resource will be left completely unchanged.

prompt: Tier 1's git-fundamentals module put *.tfstate in .gitignore mainly because state can contain plaintext secrets. What's the additional reason state should never be committed to git, even with secrets scrubbed?
choices: Git file size limits make tfstate too large to store.

State is mutable, shared truth about real infrastructure; two people applying against diverging git-tracked copies can silently corrupt or lose track of what's actually deployed, with no sane way to merge the conflict.
Terraform automatically deletes any tfstate file it finds inside a git repository.
Committing tfstate voids the provider's API credentials.
A copy of the .tf source files so they can be restored if deleted.
A log of every terraform plan and apply command that has been run.
The mapping between the resources in your configuration and the real infrastructure's IDs, attributes, and dependencies, as last known from the provider.
The provider's authentication credentials, cached for faster applies.

prompt: You lose your local terraform.tfstate (no remote backend configured), then run terraform apply again from the same .tf config, which still provisions the same bucket name. What happens?
choices: Terraform re-discovers the existing bucket on its own and updates state silently.

Terraform has no record of the bucket it already created, so it attempts to create it again - which errors out on the name collision, or, for a resource without a uniqueness constraint, silently creates a duplicate.
Terraform refuses to run any command until the state file is restored from a backup.
Terraform regenerates the exact same state file by re-reading the .tf files.

prompt: What is the relationship between variables.tf and main.tf in a parameterized Terraform configuration?
choices: variables.tf declares input parameters (name, type, optional default) that main.tf references with var.<name>, so the same configuration can be applied with different values.
variables.tf is an alternative to main.tf; only one of the two files can exist in a module.
variables.tf stores the actual secret values that get committed to git.
variables.tf is auto-generated by terraform apply and should never be edited.

prompt: Why does terraform destroy deserve particular caution compared to terraform plan?
choices: It only previews changes without touching real infrastructure.

It tears down every resource currently tracked in that state against the real provider API, and once a resource is gone there is no undo - only typing yes at the interactive prompt (or passing -auto-approve) lets it proceed.
It only deletes the local .tf files, not any provisioned infrastructure.
It requires a second, separate state file to run safely.

prompt: A terraform plan shows a resource's tags changing from Environment = "dev" to Environment = "staging", marked with a ~ and no -/+. What will terraform apply do?
choices: Destroy the existing bucket and create a brand-new one with the staging tag.
Call the provider's update API to change just the tags on the existing resource, keeping the same resource ID - an in-place update.
Nothing, because tags are metadata and are never actually applied.
Create a second, duplicate bucket alongside the first one.
